newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major says slim majority no threat to govt.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major says slim majority no threat to govt.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major said on Wednesday he did not believe his dwindling majority would affect his ability to choose a general election date.

"We have a majority in the House of Commons at the moment. On many issues we have the support of some of the other minority parties, so I think we will be able to pick our own election date," Major told the Press Association in an interview.
Major, fighting an uphill battle to win a fifth term for the ruling Conservatives who have been in office since 1979, must hold the general election by May 22.

The government has an overall majority of just one in the House of Commons. But a by-election has been called for December 12 in the safe Labour seat of Barnsley East after the death of Terry Patchett. A Labour win would eliminate Major's majority.
Another seat, Wirral South, is also vacant after the death of Conservative MP Barry Porter in November.
In Wirral South, the government had a 1992 majority of 8,183. A government victory would maintain the status quo.
But a Labour victory is not ruled out. Polls give the opposition a lead of around 20 points and Labour need a swing of 16.3 percent to take the seat.
However, the government's current majority over the Labour party alone is 52 seats, and it would take all the opposition parties to unite to force Major to go to the polls.
Major has been able in the past to rely on the Ulster Unionists from Northern Ireland in key votes.
"It isn't only the Ulster Unionists. We have had support from other quarters from time to time and that may well continue to be the case," Major told Press Association.
